questions.stem: This electron micrograph shows a single bacterium with one long, thin whip-like appendage extending from one pole. What is the primary function of that appendage?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Transfer of plasmid DNA between cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Uptake of nutrients across the membrane

explanation.summary: The polar filament is a flagellum, a protein cylinder anchored in the cell envelope that rotates to propel the bacterium; adhesion is a role of pili/fimbriae, and conjugative transfer uses sex pili.
explanation.whyCorrect: The polar filament is a flagellum, a protein cylinder anchored in the cell envelope that rotates to propel the bacterium; adhesion is a role of pili/fimbriae, and conjugative transfer uses sex pili.

questions.stem: This labeled schematic depicts a cell whose genetic material sits free in the cytoplasm as a single loop rather than inside a membrane-bound compartment. What type of cell is illustrated?

explanation.summary: The absence of a nucleus with the nucleoid/circular DNA free in the cytoplasm, plus a capsule, cell wall, pili and flagellum, identifies this as a prokaryotic bacterial cell.
explanation.whyCorrect: The absence of a nucleus with the nucleoid/circular DNA free in the cytoplasm, plus a capsule, cell wall, pili and flagellum, identifies this as a prokaryotic bacterial cell.

questions.stem: In this Ziehl-Neelsen (acid-fast) preparation, the background and most cells stain blue while a few slender, curved organisms remain bright red. What cell-wall component allows those red organisms to retain the carbol fuchsin after acid-alcohol washing?

explanation.summary: Acid-fast organisms such as Mycobacteria have waxy mycolic acids in their walls that resist decolorization by acid-alcohol, so they hold the red carbol fuchsin while other cells take up the methylene blue counterstain.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acid-fast organisms such as Mycobacteria have waxy mycolic acids in their walls that resist decolorization by acid-alcohol, so they hold the red carbol fuchsin while other cells take up the methylene blue counterstain.

questions.stem: This smear shows paired, kidney-bean-shaped diplococci that stain pink/red and lie within a host neutrophil. Why do these organisms take the pink color rather than staining purple?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are coated in waxy mycolic acids

choices.label: B
choices.text: Their wall is rich in teichoic acids

choices.label: C
choices.text: They possess only a thick polysaccharide capsule

choices.label: D
choices.text: They have a thick peptidoglycan cell wall

choices.label: E
choices.text: Their envelope has only a thin peptidoglycan layer

explanation.summary: Gram-negative diplococci lose the crystal violet during decolorization because their thin peptidoglycan sits between inner and outer membranes, so they take up the pink safranin counterstain.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gram-negative diplococci lose the crystal violet during decolorization because their thin peptidoglycan sits between inner and outer membranes, so they take up the pink safranin counterstain.

questions.stem: This schematic shows mobile DNA elements flanking a gene, allowing it to move between plasmid and chromosomal DNA. Which clinically important trait is most commonly carried between bacteria by these elements?

explanation.summary: Transposons frequently carry drug-resistance genes; when a resistance gene is flanked on both sides by transposon sequences it can be cut out and inserted elsewhere, spreading resistance between plasmids and chromosomes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Transposons frequently carry drug-resistance genes; when a resistance gene is flanked on both sides by transposon sequences it can be cut out and inserted elsewhere, spreading resistance between plasmids and chromosomes.

questions.stem: In the process shown, a donor bacterium extends a sex pilus to a recipient and transfers plasmid DNA. What is the essential requirement for this form of horizontal gene transfer?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Uptake of naked DNA from the environment

explanation.summary: Conjugation requires physical contact: the F+ donor forms a sex pilus and mating bridge with the F- recipient and transfers a single strand of the F plasmid, converting the recipient into a donor. No chromosomal DNA and no external vector is involved.
explanation.whyCorrect: Conjugation requires physical contact: the F+ donor forms a sex pilus and mating bridge with the F- recipient and transfers a single strand of the F plasmid, converting the recipient into a donor. No chromosomal DNA and no external vector is involved.

questions.stem: Here the donor's F plasmid has integrated into its chromosome before conjugation with a recipient. Compared with standard F+ conjugation, what is the key consequence of this donor state?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ribosomes are transferred to the recipient

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only the intact free plasmid is transferred

explanation.summary: In an Hfr (high-frequency recombination) donor the F plasmid is integrated in the chromosome, so transfer starting at the plasmid origin drags adjacent chromosomal genes into the recipient, allowing recombination of donor chromosomal DNA.
explanation.whyCorrect: In an Hfr (high-frequency recombination) donor the F plasmid is integrated in the chromosome, so transfer starting at the plasmid origin drags adjacent chromosomal genes into the recipient, allowing recombination of donor chromosomal DNA.

questions.stem: This sequence shows a lytic phage that mistakenly packages host DNA and delivers it to a new bacterium. How does this mechanism differ from specialized transduction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any random fragment of host DNA can be packaged and transferred

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only the phage's own viral DNA is transferred

choices.label: D
choices.text: DNA is taken up from the environment

choices.label: E
choices.text: Only DNA adjacent to a prophage integration site is transferred

explanation.summary: In generalized transduction, during lytic growth random pieces of degraded host chromosome are accidentally packaged into phage capsids, so any host gene can be moved to a recipient, unlike specialized transduction which transfers only genes flanking the prophage.
explanation.whyCorrect: In generalized transduction, during lytic growth random pieces of degraded host chromosome are accidentally packaged into phage capsids, so any host gene can be moved to a recipient, unlike specialized transduction which transfers only genes flanking the prophage.

questions.stem: In this process a temperate phage integrates into the host chromosome and later excises imprecisely, carrying adjacent bacterial genes into new hosts. Why can only specific bacterial genes be transferred this way?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only DNA flanking the prophage integration site is excised

choices.label: C
choices.text: Genes are taken up as naked DNA from the environment

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only free plasmid genes are transferred

choices.label: E
choices.text: Any random host gene can be packaged

explanation.summary: In specialized transduction the prophage integrates at a specific chromosomal site; imprecise excision picks up only the immediately adjacent bacterial DNA, so just those flanking genes can be carried to the next host.
explanation.whyCorrect: In specialized transduction the prophage integrates at a specific chromosomal site; imprecise excision picks up only the immediately adjacent bacterial DNA, so just those flanking genes can be carried to the next host.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease
questions.stem: This anatomical illustration compares the highlighted tube connecting the middle ear to the nasopharynx in an adult versus a child under 7. What property of this structure in the child explains their increased susceptibility to middle ear infections?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is shorter, narrower, and more horizontal

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is permanently occluded by adenoids

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is longer and more vertical

explanation.summary: In young children the eustachian tube is shorter, narrower, and more horizontal, allowing nasopharyngeal flora to migrate into the middle ear and impairing drainage, which predisposes to acute otitis media.
explanation.whyCorrect: In young children the eustachian tube is shorter, narrower, and more horizontal, allowing nasopharyngeal flora to migrate into the middle ear and impairing drainage, which predisposes to acute otitis media.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease
questions.stem: This labeled schematic contrasts normal vaginal epithelial cells with a cell whose surface is studded with bacteria. The stippled cell shown on the right is a diagnostic hallmark of which condition?

explanation.summary: A vaginal epithelial cell coated with adherent bacteria (obscuring its borders) is a clue cell, the microscopic hallmark of bacterial vaginosis, typically due to Gardnerella vaginalis overgrowth.
explanation.whyCorrect: A vaginal epithelial cell coated with adherent bacteria (obscuring its borders) is a clue cell, the microscopic hallmark of bacterial vaginosis, typically due to Gardnerella vaginalis overgrowth.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease
questions.stem: This clinical photograph shows the vulvar and vaginal region of a patient presenting with intense itching, erythema, and a thick white plaque. What is the most likely causative organism?

explanation.summary: The thick, white, curd-like plaque with erythema and pruritus is characteristic of vulvovaginal candidiasis caused by the yeast Candida albicans, which overgrows when normal vaginal flora is disrupted.
explanation.whyCorrect: The thick, white, curd-like plaque with erythema and pruritus is characteristic of vulvovaginal candidiasis caused by the yeast Candida albicans, which overgrows when normal vaginal flora is disrupted.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease
questions.stem: This photograph of an open mouth shows a white plaque coating the tongue and oral mucosa in a patient. Overgrowth of which organism produces this appearance?

explanation.summary: Oral thrush is an overgrowth of Candida spp. in the oral cavity, presenting as a wipeable white plaque; it is often triggered by antibiotics, inhaled steroids, dentures, or immunosuppression.
explanation.whyCorrect: Oral thrush is an overgrowth of Candida spp. in the oral cavity, presenting as a wipeable white plaque; it is often triggered by antibiotics, inhaled steroids, dentures, or immunosuppression.
